summary: Addresses requirements for accessing Public Key Infrastructure repositories with LDAPv2, to retrieve and manage PKI information such as certificates. It updates RFC 1778. It is now historic and was replaced by RFC 3494.

eli5.summary: Digital ID cards are kept in a filing cabinet. This explains how to ask the cabinet for them using an old directory lookup method. It is now retired.

questions: how to access certificates in ldap
subtitle: Using the lightweight directory protocol to retrieve and manage X.509 certificates

tldr.problem: Public key infrastructure systems need a way to store and retrieve X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists. Standard directory access methods were needed.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2559 defines a profile of LDAPv2 that lets applications query and modify a repository of PKI information including certificates and CRLs using three basic operations: read, search, and modify.
tldr.outcome: This specification was made historic and replaced by RFC 3494, which covers the same operational protocols but with an updated approach.

today: RFC 2559 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 3494.

sections.title: PKI and Directory Access
sections.content:
Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) systems need central repositories to store and retrieve X.509 certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs). Certificate users and certification authorities (CAs) must be able to search for and update this information reliably. RFC 2559 addresses this by defining how to use the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol version 2 (LDAPv2) as a standardized way to access PKI repositories.

The RFC updates RFC 1778 (which defined string representations for X.500 attributes) and provides a profile of LDAPv2 that all PKI systems can implement consistently.
sections.eli5: Digital certificates are like official ID cards. A directory system is a way to look them up. This RFC says how to use a standard lookup system to find and store these ID cards.

sections.title: The PKI Model
sections.content: RFC 2559 defines three key components: end entities (users and systems needing certificates), certification authorities (CAs that issue certificates), and the repository (the directory storing PKI data). End entities and CAs retrieve PKI information from the repository using a subset of LDAPv2 operations. CAs also populate the repository by adding, modifying and deleting PKI information. The RFC specifies which LDAP operations each participant must support.
sections.eli5: Three things work together: users asking for ID cards, official ID card makers adding them to the filing cabinet, and the filing cabinet itself. Each does different tasks.

sections.title: Three Core Operations
sections.content: The RFC defines three main operations. Repository Read retrieves PKI information from a known directory entry. It uses LDAP Bind (to authenticate), Search (with a base object and an objectClass filter), and Unbind (to disconnect). Repository Search finds entries when the exact name is not known, using broader search scopes (single level or the whole subtree) and enhanced filtering. Repository Modify allows CAs to add, delete, or modify PKI data using Add, Modify, and Delete operations, and requires authenticated Bind access.
sections.eli5: Three tasks: looking up a specific card, searching for cards that match some description, and adding or changing cards in the filing cabinet.

sections.title: Encoding Certificates and CRLs
sections.content: RFC 1778 defined string encodings for X.500 attributes, but those encodings were designed for version 1 certificates and version 1 CRLs. RFC 2559 uses version 3 certificates and version 2 CRLs, which require a different encoding. Instead of the RFC 1778 text representation, PKI attributes (like userCertificate) are encoded as octet strings containing the DER-encoded value of the certificate or CRL itself. This approach is consistent with what LDAPv3 later adopted.
sections.eli5: Certificates need to be stored in a special format when put in the directory. The RFC says to use the same compact binary format that the certificate itself uses.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content: Certificates and CRLs are digitally signed, so additional integrity protection is not required. Public access to retrieve them is generally acceptable. However, CAs making modifications require stronger security. The RFC recommends that modification operations use authenticated access and additional protection such as IPsec, TLS, or SSH tunnels. The CA must have access control permissions to manage its own certificates, modify CRL distribution points, and manage subscriber certificates it has issued. The repository is not required to provide external CAs access to its directory; this is the decision of the directory administrator.
sections.eli5: Anyone can look at ID cards because they are signed (you can tell if they are real). But adding or changing cards requires proof of who you are, and the cabinet can be locked to outside visitors.
